title: How LLMs actually work
objectives: say what the context window holds
say what a training cutoff is

steps.instruction: It does not read English. Your sentence is cut into pieces first.
body: These pieces are called tokens. A token is about four characters.
Common words are one token. Rare words get chopped up.
The model never sees your letters. It sees the pieces.
steps.keypoint: Text is cut into tokens before the model sees any of it.

steps.instruction: This asks the model to measure the text. What does it print?
steps.code:
const text = "Ottawa is in Ontario.";
console.log(ai.count(text));
steps.after: 21 characters, 6 tokens. You never guess this. You ask.
steps.why: ai.count returns tokens, not characters. 21 characters is about 6 tokens, because a token is roughly four characters.

steps.instruction: Now the whole trick. The model does exactly one thing.
body: Given every token so far, it picks the token most likely to come next.
That is it. There is no plan, no outline, no sentence it is working towards.
It picks one token, adds it to the end, and looks again.
steps.keypoint: The model chooses the next token. Then it does that again.

steps.instruction: Watch it write one sentence. Step through, one token at a time.

frames.note: Nothing written yet. The prompt was: name one city in Ontario.
It picks Ottawa. Not because it knows geography. Because those tokens most often follow that question.
Now it looks again, with Ottawa included. The next token is easy.
Again. Every step re-reads everything, including what it just wrote.
Ontario. Four tokens in, and it has never once looked ahead.
It picks a stop token, and the answer is finished.

steps.after: Five choices. No plan at any point.
steps.keypoint: Every token is chosen with the whole text so far in view, and no view of what comes next.

steps.instruction: That loop explains something you have seen. Why does a reply appear word by word instead of all at once?
opts: The app adds a typing effect to look friendly
The tokens are made one at a time, so they can be sent one at a time
The network sends text in small packets
It is waiting for you to read
steps.why: Nothing is faked. The first token exists about a second before the last one does, so an app can show it immediately.
steps.after: Every streaming AI app you have used is showing you this loop as it runs.
steps.keypoint: Replies stream because they are generated in pieces, not because of an effect.

steps.instruction: It does not always take the top choice.
body: At each step there are several likely tokens. It samples from them.
So the same question can come back worded differently.
The meaning holds. The exact words do not.
steps.keypoint: Same prompt, different words. Never compare two replies expecting a match.

steps.instruction: Sending a question, and reading the reply.
steps.after: That is a real reply object. Same shape the real API returns.
body: The reply is an object. The words are at content[0].text, never at reply itself.

steps.instruction: Everything it can see at once has a name: the context window.
body: The context window holds your instructions, your question, and what it has written so far.
That is all it has. Nothing from last week, nothing from another user, nothing from your database.
It is measured in tokens, and it has a ceiling.
steps.keypoint: The context window is everything the model can see. If it is not in there, it does not exist.

steps.instruction: Which of these can the model see?
steps.after: Your database is invisible until you put some of it in the prompt yourself.
steps.keypoint: You choose what goes in the window. It cannot reach for anything else.
skills: say what the context window holds

steps.instruction: One more limit: it learned from text up to a date, and then stopped.
body: That date is the training cutoff.
Anything after it, the model has never read. Yesterday's news, your new code, this morning's score.
It will still answer. It just has nothing real to answer from.
steps.keypoint: Training cutoff: it read up to a date and stopped. After that, it is guessing.

steps.instruction: Which of these can the model answer from what it learned?
opts: What did I score on today's quiz?
What is in my notes app?
What is the capital of Canada?
What happened in the news this morning?
steps.why: The capital of Canada was in the training text and has not changed. The other three are either after the cutoff or private to you, so the only honest source is your own prompt.
steps.after: Three of those four are answerable, but only if YOU put the answer in the prompt first.
steps.keypoint: Public and old, it may know. Recent or yours, you have to supply.

steps.instruction: A chat four turns in. What does this print?
steps.code:
const conversation = "My name is Ada. Hello Ada. What is in Ontario? Ottawa is.";
console.log(ai.count(conversation));
steps.after: Every one of those is resent on the next call, because nothing is remembered.
steps.why: It counts the tokens in the whole conversation, because all of it is resent on the next call. Nothing is remembered.
